fields.Front: Describe twisted pair: construction, why it is twisted, where it dominates, and the Cat 5 vs Cat 6 rates.
fields.Back:
Two insulated copper wires twisted around each other; twisting reduces electrical interference from neighbouring pairs.
Cheapest, most common guided medium; dominates LANs.
Category 5: 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps Ethernet. Category 6: 10 Gbps Ethernet.

fields.Front: Describe coaxial cable: construction and its three key properties.
fields.Back:
Two concentric copper conductors.
1) Bidirectional.
2) Broadband: multiple frequency channels on one cable (FDM), 100s of Mbps per channel.
3) Can act as a shared guided medium: the medium of cable TV and cable Internet (HFC).

fields.Front: Why is fiber the preferred long-haul / backbone medium? Give its three advantages.
fields.Back:
Glass fiber carrying light pulses (each pulse = one bit).
1) High-speed point-to-point transmission: tens to hundreds of Gbps.
2) Low error rate: repeaters can be spaced far apart.
3) Immune to electromagnetic noise.

fields.Front: Characterize wireless radio links: how the signal travels, duplex/broadcast nature, and the three propagation-environment effects.
fields.Back:
Signal carried in the electromagnetic spectrum, no physical wire.
Broadcast and half-duplex (sender to receiver, one direction at a time).
Propagation effects: 1) reflection, 2) obstruction by objects, 3) interference.

fields.Text: {{c1::Guided}} media: signals propagate in a solid medium (copper, fiber, coax). {{c1::Unguided}} media: signals propagate freely (e.g., radio). A bit propagates between {{c1::transmitter/receiver}} pairs; the physical link is what lies between them.
Guided-media rates: Cat 5 twisted pair {{c1::100 Mbps / 1 Gbps}}; Cat 6 {{c1::10 Gbps}}; coax {{c1::100s of Mbps per channel}}; fiber {{c1::10s-100s of Gbps}}, each light pulse a bit.

Radio link types and rates: terrestrial microwave {{c1::up to 45 Mbps per channel}}; WiFi WLAN {{c1::up to 100s of Mbps}}; 4G cellular {{c1::~tens of Mbps}}; satellite {{c1::up to 45 Mbps per channel, 270 ms delay}}.

Satellite links: {{c1::geostationary}} satellites orbit at {{c1::36,000 km}}, giving a signal propagation delay of about {{c1::280 ms}} (the slides say 270 ms) while carrying up to {{c1::hundreds of Mbps}}; they also underpin {{c1::GPS}}. {{c1::LEO}} satellites (e.g. Starlink) orbit far lower with a round-trip delay of about {{c1::10 ms}}, but need {{c1::many satellites}} for continuous coverage. (Kurose 9th ed. §1.2.2)

Textbook only (Kurose §1.2.2): fibre has very low attenuation up to {{c1::100 km}} and is {{c1::very hard to tap}}; its drawback is the {{c1::cost of optical transmitters, receivers and switches}}. Long-haul link speeds use the {{c1::Optical Carrier (OC)}} standard, where OC-n equals {{c1::n x 51.8 Mbps}}, running from OC-1 up to {{c1::OC-768}} at 39.8 Gbps.
fields.Extra: Also from the book: the labour cost of installing a physical link is often orders of magnitude higher than the cable itself, which is why builders pull twisted pair, fibre and coax into every room at once.
